q: What is PHP?
a: PHP (Hypertext Preprocessor) is a widely-used open-source server-side scripting language designed for web development. It can be embedded into HTML and runs on the server, generating dynamic page content. PHP is loosely typed, interpreted, and supports object-oriented programming.

q: How do you declare variables in PHP?
a: Variables in PHP start with a $ sign followed by the name. They are loosely typed — no type declaration is required. Example: $name = "John";. PHP 7+ supports typed properties in classes and PHP 8+ adds union types.

q: What is the difference between echo and print?
a: echo can output multiple strings separated by commas and is slightly faster. print returns 1 so it can be used in expressions. Both are language constructs (not functions), so parentheses are optional.

q: Explain == vs === in PHP.
a: == (loose equality) coerces types before comparing, e.g. "5" == 5 is true. === (strict equality) checks both value and type, so "5" === 5 is false. Always prefer === for predictable comparisons.

q: Explain PHP 8 attributes and their use.
a: PHP 8.0+ attributes (annotations) add structured metadata to classes, methods, properties, etc. They use the #[Attribute] syntax. Attributes are read via reflection ($ref->getAttributes()). Laravel uses them for route definitions, event listeners, and model casting. Example: #[Route('get', '/dashboard')].

q: What are fibers in PHP?
a: Fibers (PHP 8.1+) are lightweight coroutines for cooperative multitasking. A fiber can be suspended (Fiber::suspend()) and resumed ($fiber->resume()) from the main execution context. Unlike full coroutines, fibers don't require an event loop — they provide interruptible function execution. Useful for implementing generators, async iterators, and cooperative task scheduling without a framework.

q: What are PHP 8.4 property hooks?
a: PHP 8.4 introduced property hooks, allowing custom get/set logic for properties without writing separate methods. Syntax: public string $name { get => ...; set => ...; }. Also added asymmetric visibility (public private(set) string $email). These replace boilerplate getter/setter methods and enable computed properties, validation on set, and lazy loading — reducing the need for __get/__set magic methods.

q: Explain the SOLID principles in depth.
a:
Single Responsibility: each class has one reason to change.
Open/Closed: open for extension, closed for modification (use interfaces/abstract classes).
Liskov Substitution: subtypes must be substitutable for their base types (contract fidelity).
Interface Segregation: many specific interfaces > one general interface.
Dependency Inversion: depend on abstractions, not concretions.

In Laravel: SRP → controller/service separation. OCP → strategy pattern for payment gateways. LSP → collections and contracts. ISP → small contract interfaces. DIP → IoC container resolves abstractions. Violating SOLID leads to rigid, hard-to-test code.

q: What are magic methods and their advanced use cases?
a:
PHP magic methods start with __:
__construct(), __destruct() — lifecycle
__call()/__callStatic() — method overloading (used by facades)
__get()/__set() — property overloading (used by Eloquent models for dynamic attributes)
__invoke() — callable objects (invokable controllers, route actions)
__toString() — string casting (presenters)
__serialize()/__unserialize() — custom serialization (queues, cache)
__clone() — deep copy control

Senior insight: overusing magic methods hurts IDE support and static analysis. Use them intentionally — Eloquent's __get is elegant; custom __call for proxies is powerful but test with care.

q: Compare Repository vs Active Record patterns. When do you use each?
a:
Active Record (Eloquent): each model handles both data and persistence. Simple, rapid development, ideal for CRUD apps where business logic is thin. Tight coupling to the ORM.

Repository: abstracts data access behind an interface (UserRepositoryInterface). Swap implementations (Eloquent, Redis, external API) without changing business logic. Enables unit testing with mocks.

When to use Repository: complex domain logic, multiple data sources, CQRS, need to swap storage, hexagonal architecture, or when you want to decouple from Eloquent entirely.

When Active Record is fine: simple CRUD, prototypes, Bounded Contexts where the model's persistence isn't complex. Laravel's Eloquent is extremely productive — don't abstract prematurely.

q: Explain the Strategy pattern with a real Laravel example.
a:
The Strategy pattern defines interchangeable algorithms via a common interface. Each strategy encapsulates a specific behavior, and the context delegates to the selected strategy.

Laravel example: payment gateways.
interface PaymentGateway { public function charge($amount); }
class StripeGateway implements PaymentGateway { ... }
class PayPalGateway implements PaymentGateway { ... }

Context resolves via container: $gateway = app(PaymentGateway::class); bound in service provider based on config. Laravel's mail drivers, cache backends, filesystem disks, and queue drivers all use this pattern. Benefit: adding a new gateway means adding a class — zero changes to existing code (OCP).

q: How does Laravel's middleware implement the Decorator pattern?
a:
Laravel's middleware pipeline uses a chain-of-responsibility + decorator hybrid. Each middleware wraps the request handling:

function handle($request, Closure $next) {
// before decorator
$response = $next($request);
// after decorator
return $response;
}

The Pipeline class passes the request through each middleware sequentially. Each middleware can modify the request before passing it down, and modify the response coming back — classic decorator behavior.

Real-world: ThrottleMiddleware decorates by rate-checking. EncryptCookies decrypts on the way in, encrypts on the way out. Middleware order matters — put TrimStrings before ThrottleRequests.

q: Explain Laravel's service container internals. How does auto-resolution work?
a:
The service container (Illuminate\Container\Container) is Laravel's IoC container. It can:

1. Auto-resolution: when a type-hinted class is needed, the container uses Reflection to inspect the constructor, recursively resolves all dependencies, and returns the instance.

2. Binding: $container->bind(Interface::class, Concrete::class) maps abstractions to concretions. Resolved fresh each time.

3. Singletons: $container->singleton() returns the same instance on subsequent resolutions.

4. Instance: $container->instance() binds a pre-built object.

5. Contextual binding: when(PhotoController::class)->needs(Filesystem::class)->give(function() { return Storage::disk('local'); });

Senior insight: the container is NOT a service locator in practice — it's used for dependency injection. Avoid app() in controllers; prefer constructor injection. The container's rebinding callbacks enable extensibility for packages.

q: Explain Laravel's Pipeline pattern and its uses beyond middleware.
a:
Illuminate\Pipeline\Pipeline passes a value through a series of pipes (callables/classes). Each pipe receives the value and a $next closure.

Uses beyond HTTP middleware:
1. Queued job middleware: wrap job execution with rate limiting or logging
2. Mail sending pipeline: transform mailables through formatting pipes
3. Validation pipelines: custom rules that chain
4. Request preprocessing: normalize input before controller

Code:
app(Pipeline::class)
->send($request)
->through([TrimStrings::class, RemoveEmpty::class])
->then(fn($req) => $this->process($req));

Pipeline enables clean separation of cross-cutting concerns without inheritance. Each pipe is independently testable.

q: What major architectural changes were introduced in Laravel 11+?
a:
Laravel 11+ introduced a significantly leaner skeleton:

1. Fewer service providers: default providers reduced from 9 to 3 (AppServiceProvider, RouteServiceProvider removed — routing is now in bootstrap/app.php)

2. No separate HTTP/Kernel classes: middleware is configured in bootstrap/app.php via ->withMiddleware()

3. No separate Console/Kernel: commands registered via ->withCommands()

4. SQLite by default: zero-config database for new projects

5. Health routing: /up endpoint for load balancers

6. Graceful encryption key rotation: APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS env var

Impact: faster bootstrap, less boilerplate, more convention over configuration. Upgrading existing apps is optional but recommended for new projects.

q: What are deferred service providers and when should you use them?
a:
Deferred service providers delay registration until their services are first requested, reducing request overhead. They implement Illuminate\Contracts\Support\DeferrableProvider and provide a provides() method listing the bindings.

When to use: for providers that register services used only in specific code paths (console commands, mail, notifications, queue jobs).

Example:
class MailServiceProvider extends ServiceProvider implements DeferrableProvider {
public function register() { ... }
public function provides() { return ['mailer', 'mail.manager']; }
}

Senior insight: Laravel 11+ auto-detects deferred providers. Profile before optimizing — premature deferral adds complexity. Most apps don't need it unless you have 50+ providers or high-traffic API endpoints.

q: What are macros in Laravel?
a:
Macros allow adding methods to core Laravel classes at runtime via the Macroable trait. Classes like Str, Collection, Request, and Response are Macroable.

Example:
Str::macro('partNumber', function($prefix) {
return $prefix . '-' . strtoupper(Str::random(6));
});

Define macros in the boot() method of a service provider. Macros are testable via mocking. Senior pattern: package authors use macros to extend Laravel without modifying vendor files.

q: What are route model bindings and how do you customize them?
a:
Route model binding automatically injects Eloquent model instances into controller methods. When a route parameter matches a model's primary key (usually id), Laravel fetches the model and passes it to the controller.

Implicit: /users/{user} → resolve by ID. /users/{user:slug} → resolve by slug column.

Explicit: in AppServiceProvider::boot():
Route::bind('user', fn($value) => User::where('slug', $value)->firstOrFail());

Senior tip: use Route::model('user', User::class) for custom keys. Always eager-load relationships in route bindings when needed to avoid N+1.

q: What is eager loading and the N+1 problem?
a:
N+1 problem: querying N items and then accessing a relation per item causes N extra queries. For 100 posts with author access → 1 (posts) + 100 (authors) = 101 queries.

Eager loading: Post::with('author')->get() → 2 queries total (one for posts, one for authors).

Nested eager loading: with('author.profile', 'comments.user')

Senior tools:
• Model::preventLazyLoading() in local/dev to catch N+1 at dev time
• Laravel Debugbar or Telescope to monitor query counts
• load() for lazy eager loading after query
• loadCount(), loadSum() for aggregates without loading relations

q: How do you optimize Eloquent performance for high-traffic applications?
a:
1. Query optimization:
• Use select() — never fetch columns you don't need
• Eager load (with()) to eliminate N+1
• cursor() for memory-efficient iteration of large datasets (uses generators)
• chunk() / chunkById() for batch processing

2. Database:
• Add indexes for WHERE, JOIN, ORDER BY, and foreign key columns
• Use explain() to analyze query plans
• Consider read replicas for reporting queries

3. Caching:
• Cache::remember() for expensive queries
• Cache tags for group invalidation
• Model caching with remember() on collections

4. Advanced:
• Use simplePaginate() or cursorPaginate() instead of paginate() on large datasets (avoids count query)
• withCount() / withExists() for aggregates without loading relations
• Avoid N+1 in serialization: use API Resources with conditional eager loading

q: What is Laravel Octane and when would you use it?
a:
Laravel Octane serves the application in-memory using Swoole or RoadRunner, booting the framework once and handling hundreds of requests in the same process. This eliminates the boot time overhead per request.

Benefits:
• 10-50x throughput increase
• Shared in-memory state (config, routes cached once)

Trade-offs:
• Memory leaks from static properties persist across requests
• Must avoid $_GET/$_POST globals — use request facade
• Database connections and other singletons need careful management
• Requires Swoole/RoadRunner expertise

When to use: high-traffic APIs (1M+ requests/day), real-time apps with WebSockets (via Swoole's coroutine support), when every ms of latency matters. Skip it for standard CRUD apps behind Nginx+PHP-FPM — it's overkill.

q: What are signed URLs and how do they work?
a:
Signed URLs are HMAC-signed URLs that verify the URL hasn't been tampered with. Laravel generates a signature using the app key and appends it as a signature query parameter.

Generation:
URL::signedRoute('unsubscribe', ['user' => 1]);
URL::temporarySignedRoute('verify', now()->addHours(24), ['id' => 1]);

Verification:
$request->hasValidSignature() middleware

Use cases: email verification links, password reset, unsubscribe links, public file downloads, payment receipts — any link that needs to be verifiable without requiring authentication.

Security note: always use temporarySignedRoute with expiration for sensitive operations. The signature uses SHA-256 HMAC — it's cryptographically secure.

q: Compare Laravel's authentication strategies: Sanctum vs Passport vs Jetstream vs Fortify.
a:
Sanctum: lightweight token-based auth for SPAs and mobile apps. Uses cookie-based session auth for SPAs (same-domain) and API tokens for mobile/third-party. Built-in, zero config. Best for most Laravel apps.

Passport: full OAuth2 server (Authorization Code, Client Credentials, Password Grant, Personal Access Tokens). Heavy, complex. Use only when you need OAuth2 — third-party API access, multi-service architecture.

Fortify: headless auth backend (login, registration, password reset, 2FA) without UI. Provides routes and controllers — you build the frontend. Use with Inertia/Vue/React SPA.

Jetstream: opinionated Laravel starter kit using Fortify + Tailwind + Livewire/Inertia. Includes teams, 2FA, API tokens, profile management. Quick start for new apps.

Senior recommendation: Start with Sanctum. Add Passport only if you need OAuth2. Use Fortify for headless backends.

q: What are the top security concerns in Laravel applications and how do you mitigate them?
a:
1. SQL Injection: Eloquent uses PDO parameter binding — safe by default. Raw queries must use bound parameters: DB::select('...', [$value]).

2. XSS (Cross-Site Scripting): Blade's {{ }} escapes via htmlspecialchars(). Never use {!! !!} with user input. Apply CSP headers.

3. CSRF: @csrf in forms. Exempt safe endpoints (webhooks) carefully. VerifyCsrfToken middleware protects state-changing requests.

4. Mass Assignment: define $fillable or $guarded in all models. Never pass all request input to create().

5. Rate Limiting: apply throttle:60,1 middleware on API routes. Use RateLimiter for per-user limits.

6. Security Headers: X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, Strict-Transport-Security via middleware or Nginx config.

7. Dependency Scanning: composer audit — run in CI. Use Dependabot or Renovate for automated updates.

q: Design a secure API authentication system for a multi-tenant SaaS platform.
a:
Architecture:

1. Authentication: Sanctum with personal access tokens, scoped by tenant. Each token stored in personal_access_tokens with abilities JSON column (['tenant:123', 'scope:read']).

2. Multi-tenant guard: custom guard that resolves tenant from API token's abilities. Middleware validates token has both auth + tenant scope.

3. Rate limiting: per-token, per-tenant, per-endpoint tiers (free: 100/h, pro: 10000/h). Implement via RateLimiter::for('api') with Redis backend.

4. API key rotation: Token::rotate() invalidates old, issues new. Old key works for 24h grace period.

5. Audit logging: all API requests logged (user, tenant, endpoint, IP, timestamp) to dedicated audit table with 90-day retention.

6. Encryption at rest: PII columns encrypted via Laravel's Castable attribute with AES-256-GCM.

7. Webhook security: verify signatures with HMAC-SHA256, support retries with idempotency keys (Idempotency-Key header).

q: Design a RESTful API versioning strategy for a Laravel application.
a:
Three strategies:

1. URL prefix (/api/v1/users, /api/v2/users): most explicit, easy to route. Use Route::prefix('v1')->group(...). Simple but URL pollution.

2. Header-based (Accept: application/vnd.app.v1+json): cleaner URLs, harder to test. Requires custom route matcher or middleware.

3. Subdomain (v1.api.example.com): clean separation, infrastructure complexity.

Recommendation: URL prefix for simplicity. Keep versioned code in separate directories:

app/Http/Controllers/Api/V1/
app/Http/Resources/V1/
app/Http/Requests/Api/V1/

Senior practices:
• Never break existing clients — add fields, don't remove
• Deprecate with Deprecation header + sunset date
• Maintain old versions for minimum 6 months
• Use API Resources to transform v1 vs v2 responses separately

q: Design a high-throughput job processing system with Laravel queues.
a:
Architecture:

1. Driver: Redis (or SQS for serverless). Redis is fastest for Laravel — use phpredis extension, not predis.

2. Workers: php artisan queue:work redis --queue=high,default,low --tries=3 --sleep=3. Run via Supervisor (one process per queue per core).

3. Job batching: Bus::batch([...])->then($finally)->dispatch() for parallel processing + completion callback.

4. Rate limiting: Job middleware: RateLimiter::for('jobs')->limit(100). RateLimited middleware prevents API throttling.

5. Monitoring: Horizon for Redis queue dashboards, failure tracking, auto-scaling workers.

6. Failure handling: failed_jobs table with 7-day retention. Failed jobs sent to Slack via Queue::failing() event.

7. Pipeline: chain jobs with Bus::chain([...])->dispatch() for sequential processing.

q: Design a multi-tenant SaaS application with Laravel.
a:
Two approaches:

Single database (row-level):
• All tenants share one database. Each table has tenant_id column.
• Global scope: TenantScope auto-filters where('tenant_id', currentTenant()) on all queries.
• Pros: simple infrastructure, easy migrations. Cons: data isolation risk, harder to scale.

Multi-database (database-per-tenant):
• Each tenant gets their own database. Central tenants table maps domains to databases.
• Middleware resolves tenant, sets config('database.connections.tenant.database') dynamically.
• Pros: strong isolation, can backup/restore per tenant. Cons: complex migrations, higher resource usage.

Key considerations:
• Domain routing: Route::domain('{tenant}.app.com') or header-based
• Cache isolation: prefix cache keys with tenant ID
• Queue isolation: separate queue per tenant or use tenant_id in job metadata
• File storage: directories per tenant on S3 (tenants/{id}/)
• Testing: ensure tenant-scoped tests don't leak data between test suites

q: Design a full-text search system for a high-traffic Laravel application.
a:
Recommended stack: MeiliSearch (self-hosted or Cloud) + Laravel Scout.

Architecture:

1. Indexing: add Searchable trait to models. Override toSearchableArray() to include related data:
return array_merge($this->toArray(), ['category' => $this->category->name]);

2. Queue indexing: Scout auto-queues index updates via the queue connection. Configure scout.queue for async processing.

3. Search endpoint:
Product::search($query)
->where('category_id', $categoryId)
->where('price', '<', 100)
->orderBy('relevance')
->paginate(20);

4. Filterable attributes: configure in MeiliSearch settings for category_id, price, in_stock.

5. Typo tolerance: MeiliSearch handles typos by default — configure minWordSizeForTypos per use case.

6. Performance:
• Index only searchable fields — don't index raw HTML or logs
• Use separate index per locale for multilingual apps
• Re-index without downtime: build new index, swap atomically
• Monitor search analytics to tune ranking rules

q: Design a blog system with categories, tags, and comments — covering edge cases.
a:
Models:
• Post (belongsTo Category, belongsToMany Tag, morphMany Comment)
• Category (hasMany posts)
• Tag (belongsToMany posts)
• Comment (morphTo commentable) — allows commenting on posts + pages

Features:
• SoftDeletes on Post — archive without losing comments
• Form Request validation with unique slug generation
• Policy for authorization — only author can edit
• Eager load relationships on index: with(['category', 'tags', 'comments.user'])
• View composer for sidebar (recent posts, categories with counts)

Edge cases:
• Unauthorized edit attempts → 403 via policy
• Empty tags → allow saving without tags
• Soft-deleted posts → exclude from queries with global scope
• Duplicate slugs → append UUID suffix
• Orphaned comments when post deleted → SoftDeletes preserves them; show "Post deleted" message

q: Design a shopping cart that persists across guest sessions and login merge.
a:
Approach:

Database:
Cart model: user_id (nullable), session_id, product_id, quantity, created_at.

CartService:
• addItem(productId, quantity) — upsert by product
• removeItem(productId)
• getTotal() — sum of (price × quantity)
• clear()

Guest flow: cart stored with session_id only. Data loaded on every page via ViewComposer or middleware.

Login merge: on Login event, call CartService::mergeCarts(sessionCart, userCart):
• For each guest item: if user has same product, sum quantities (capped at stock). Else, attach to user.
• Delete session cart after merge.

Edge cases:
• Product deleted during session → show "Unavailable" with remove option
• Quantity overflow → limit to stock
• Duplicate items — upsert logic prevents duplicates
• Concurrent sessions → last-write-wins (acceptable for carts)

q: Design a real-time chat system with Laravel Reverb.
a:
Architecture:

Backend:
• Conversation (belongsToMany users via conversation_user with last_read_at)
• Message (belongsTo user, belongsTo conversation)
• Broadcasting: MessageSent event implements ShouldBroadcast on private-conversation.{id} channel.
• Authorization channel: Broadcast::channel('private-conversation.{id}', fn($user, $id) => $user->conversations->contains($id));

Reverb:
• Self-hosted WebSocket server. Scales horizontally with Redis pub/sub.
• Run via Supervisor: php artisan reverb:start --host=0.0.0.0 --port=8080

Frontend (Laravel Echo):
Echo.private('conversation.' + id)
.listen('MessageSent', (e) => appendMessage(e.message));

Typing indicator: debounced 2-second broadcast. Clear on send.

Edge cases:
• Offline messages → stored in DB, pushed when user reconnects (presence channels)
• Concurrent connections → Reverb handles via channel auth
• Message ordering → rely on message ID (auto-increment), not client timestamps
• File attachments → queue thumbnails via ShouldQueue broadcast

q: Design a multi-region, high-availability deployment for a Laravel application.
a:
Architecture:

Infrastructure:
• 3 regions (US, EU, APAC) behind a global load balancer (AWS Global Accelerator / Cloudflare)
• Each region: autoscaling group (min 3, max 20) behind ALB
• Database: Aurora Global Database (1 primary in US, read replicas in EU/APAC)
• Redis: ElastiCache Global Datastore for cross-region cache
• Session: Redis with read-replica failover
• Queue: SQS (global) — FIFO for order-sensitive jobs
• Files: S3 with Cross-Region Replication + CloudFront CDN

Laravel config:
• SESSION_DRIVER=redis, CACHE_STORE=redis
• Queue: SQS driver
• Octane on RoadRunner for in-memory boot
• Read/write DB connections: 'read' => ['host' => $readHost], 'write' => ['host' => $writeHost]

Deployment:
• CI/CD: GitHub Actions → build Docker image → push to ECR → ECS rolling update
• Zero-downtime: blue/green deployment with health checks
• Migrations: run in CI before deploy, use --isolated for concurrent safety

q: Design a caching strategy for a Laravel API serving 10M requests/day.
a:
Layered caching strategy:

1. HTTP caching (Edge/CDN):
• CloudFront/Varnish for GET endpoints
• Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300
• Purge on model saved/deleted events via cache tags

2. Application cache (Redis):
• Cache::remember('product:'.$id, 300, fn() => ...)
• Cache tags for group invalidation: Cache::tags(['products', 'category:'.$catId])->flush()
• Cache-aside: app checks cache first, falls back to DB, writes to cache
• Write-through: on update, write both DB + cache

3. Query cache:
• remember() on expensive queries: Product::where(...)->remember(60)->get()
• Use select() to minimize data transferred from Redis

4. Full-page cache:
• Static responses (docs, landing pages) served from CDN
• Dynamic pages use laravel-page-cache with Varnish/NGINX

5. Invalidation strategy:
• Event-driven: ProductSaved → Cache::tags(['products'])->flush()
• Stale-while-revalidate: serve stale cache, refresh in background
• Versioned keys: increment cache version on deploy (atomic rollover)

q: Design a multi-channel notification system with Laravel.
a:
Approach:

1. Notification class: php artisan make:notification InvoicePaid
2. Channels: via($notifiable) returns ['mail', 'database', 'vonage', 'slack']
3. Each channel: define toMail(), toDatabase(), toVonage(), toSlack() methods
4. Queued by default: add ShouldQueue interface
5. User preferences: notification_preferences JSON column on User — checked in via()

Database notification: stored in notifications table. Read/unread tracked. Show in-app bell icon.

Edge cases:
• Rate limiting: implement withRateLimiting() to avoid API provider throttling
• Notification logging: NotificationLog model for audit trail
• Opt-out: per-channel unsubscribe links in email
• Batch sending: use jobs with tries=3, backoff for retry logic
